query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy’s robust strength–ductility balance under varying temperatures and strain rates is governed by a dynamic deformation mechanism in which strain-induced amorphization at grain boundaries transiently refines the microstructure. This effect enhances dislocation pinning (and hence strain hardening) while maintaining ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified single-phase solid solution of Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled mechanical testing varying strain rate (from quasi-static to high strain rate) and temperature (spanning cryogenic to elevated temperatures) in an ultra‐high vacuum environment to avoid extrinsic surface effects.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under conditions where dynamic structural changes (limited to internal, kinetic processes such as amorphization or dynamic grain refinement) can occur without full recrystallization or diffusion-driven phase changes. Comparison with the Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi under identical conditions is recommended.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of ultra‐nanocrystalline and/or amorphous grain boundary layers that emerge dynamically during deformation
generation.mechanism: Under increased strain rates and/or non-ambient temperatures, local stress concentrations induce dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries. This transient formation of nanoscale, disordered regions increases dislocation pinning and promotes strain hardening, thereby offsetting thermal softening or dynamic instability and preserving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline test (room temperature, moderate strain rate) exhibiting a uniform grain size, tests under higher strain rates or varied temperatures will show a refined, heterogeneous grain structure with detectable amorphous intergranular films that correlate with enhanced strain hardening rates while maintaining comparable ductility. In a controlled comparison, the Co‐free alloy should demonstrate these dynamic microstructural changes more distinctly than its Co-containing counterpart.
generation.baseline: The Co‐free alloy deformed at room temperature and moderate strain rate, which shows a uniform grain structure with typical dislocation-based plasticity.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in regimes where deformation kinetics activate dynamic amorphization (i.e., intermediate strain rates and temperatures below those causing diffusion-controlled recrystallization). It may not apply in conditions that either allow complete recovery/recrystallization or where other mechanisms (e.g., twinning) predominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the dynamic amorphization model is supported by analogous behavior in CoCrFeMnNi alloys (e.g., inverse Hall–Petch regimes), the precise role and extent of this mechanism in the Co‐free variant remains to be quantitatively established. Potential contributions from other dynamic processes, such as the onset of nano-twinning, cannot be completely excluded.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ high-resolution TEM tensile testing of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy across a range of strain rates and temperatures. Simultaneously, conduct equivalent tests on the Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi alloy as a control. Quantify grain size distributions, detect the presence of amorphous intergranular films, and correlate these with strain hardening rates from stress–strain measurements.
measurements: Grain size distribution via TEM imaging
Identification of amorphous versus crystalline regions at grain boundaries (using diffraction patterns and high-resolution imaging)
Stress–strain curves to extract strain hardening rates
Dislocation density counts and possibly in-situ tracking of microstructural evolution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If in-situ observations do not reveal significant dynamic formation of amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline grain boundary regions correlating with enhanced strain hardening (or if similar effects are observed equally in both Co-free and Co-containing alloys under identical conditions), then the hypothesis that dynamic amorphization is the dominant mechanism behind the favorable strength–ductility balance in the Co-free alloy would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
